walkthroughs.body_html:
Working as a Physicist — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Working as a Physicist brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Working as a Physicist.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A car travels 4 km north then 3 km east. What is its displacement magnitude?
options: 7 km
5 km
1 km
25 km

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
options: Acceleration
Momentum
Kinetic energy
Weight

mcqs.q: Why do transformers only work with alternating current?
options: Transformers work with DC too, just less efficiently.
Voltage measures how many electrons are stored in a battery.
A transformer needs a changing magnetic flux in the core; DC produces a steady flux and so no emf is induced in the secondary.
DC cannot enter a transformer because the iron core blocks it.

mcqs.q: What does voltage (potential difference) across a component represent?
options: Voltage is the 'amount of electricity' flowing through the wire.
The energy transferred per unit charge passing through that component.
DC cannot enter a transformer because the iron core blocks it.
Voltage measures how many electrons are stored in a battery.

mcqs.q: If air resistance is ignored, which falls faster: a heavy ball or a light ball dropped from the same height?
options: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects because gravity pulls more on them.
The lighter ball falls faster because it has less inertia.
Both fall at the same rate because gravitational acceleration is independent of mass.
DC cannot enter a transformer because the iron core blocks it.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Acceleration”?
options: Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Velocity”?
options: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vector”?
options: The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Displacement”?
options: The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Resolving vectors”?
options: Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Scalar”?
options: A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
